candidates.label: Mount of Olives
candidates.support: Wikidata's coordinate for the ridge is corroborated by OpenBible.info's independently recorded point for the same feature.

summary.text: The Mount of Olives is the ridge east of Jerusalem's Old City, separated from the Temple Mount by the Kidron Valley, with its summit directly overlooking the Temple precinct. Its name comes from the olive groves that, then as now, covered its terraced slopes; its eastern side descends through the villages of Bethphage and Bethany toward the Judean wilderness and, further on, Jericho and the Jordan Valley. No temple, synagogue or other major building stood on the ridge itself in this period; the Kidron Valley at its foot already held rock-cut tombs, part of a long-used burial ground.

history.text: The Gospels describe Jesus and his disciples regularly on the Mount of Olives: travelers coming up from Jericho passed its villages on the way into Jerusalem, Jesus sent two disciples from Bethphage to fetch a colt for his entry into the city, and he taught there, including the discourse later called the Olivet Discourse. Luke says that during his final days in Jerusalem he spent his nights on the mount, and all three Synoptic Gospels record him going out to the mount, to Gethsemane, for his last prayer on the night of his arrest; Acts records the disciples returning to Jerusalem from the mount after his ascension.

The Old Testament already names the ridge: 2 Samuel describes King David fleeing over it during Absalom's revolt, and Zechariah's prophecy pictures a coming day when "his feet will stand... on the Mount of Olives," imagery later linked to the mount's Jewish and Christian associations with a final judgment.

Today the ridge carries several churches marking Gospel scenes, among them the Franciscan sanctuaries of Bethphage and Dominus Flevit ("the Lord wept"), the Church of the Pater Noster, and the Chapel of the Ascension near the summit, alongside the large Mount of Olives Jewish Cemetery that covers much of the slope. The summit gives one of the best-known views over Jerusalem's Old City, with the Temple Mount directly below; to the north, the separate rise of Mount Scopus now carries a campus of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

scripture.textWEB: They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.
When they came near to Jerusalem and came to Bethsphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples,
As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, “Tell us, when will these things be? What is the sign of your coming, and of the end of the age?”
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
When they came near to Jerusalem, to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples
As he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked him privately,
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
When he came near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples,
As he was now getting near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen,
Every day Jesus was teaching in the temple, and every night he would go out and spend the night on the mountain that is called Olivet.
He came out and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives. His disciples also followed him.
but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.
Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away.

otConnections.note: Zechariah's prophecy that 'his feet will stand in that day on the Mount of Olives' (a coming day of the Lord) is widely noted as background for the mount's later Jewish and Christian eschatological associations.
David's flight over the Mount of Olives during Absalom's revolt is the earliest narrative use of the mountain as a named place on a route out of Jerusalem.
